title: Acts 9:1–19
context: Saul, still breathing threats against the disciples, obtains letters to arrest followers of the Way in Damascus. Near the city a light from heaven flashes around him, and he hears Jesus ask why Saul is persecuting him. Blinded, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a reluctant Ananias to him, calling Saul a chosen vessel to carry his name to Gentiles, kings, and Israel. Ananias lays hands on him, Saul regains his sight, is filled with the Spirit, and is baptized.

verses.text: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
verses.arminianNotes: Saul is still breathing threats and murder against the disciples. Arminian readers see a man fully committed to his course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a sinner in open rebellion, which makes the coming grace all the more striking.

verses.text: and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: He requests letters to arrest any belonging to the Way. Arminian commentators note the early name for the faith, the Way.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see Saul’s zeal directed against Christ himself.

verses.text: As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
verses.arminianNotes: Near Damascus a light from heaven suddenly flashes around him. Arminian readers see God interrupting Saul’s path unexpectedly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sovereign grace taking the initiative without any request from Saul.

verses.text: He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
verses.arminianNotes: He falls and hears, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Arminian expositors see Jesus addressing Saul personally and calling him to account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see Christ’s union with his church: to persecute believers is to persecute him.

verses.text: He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
verses.arminianNotes: “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Arminian readers see Saul confronted with the truth he had resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the moment of revelation that overturns Saul’s understanding.

verses.text: But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.” Arminian commentators see Saul called to obey and to respond in action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see Christ directing the next steps of the one he has seized.

verses.text: The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
verses.arminianNotes: His companions hear the sound but see no one. Arminian readers note that the call is personal to Saul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an effectual call aimed at one man, while others nearby are not converted.

verses.text: Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul rises but sees nothing and is led by the hand. Arminian expositors see the proud persecutor humbled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see a picture of spiritual blindness before illumination.

verses.text: He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
verses.arminianNotes: For three days he neither sees, eats, nor drinks. Arminian readers see a time of repentance and reflection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inward work of conviction preparing him for what follows.

verses.text: Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord speaks to Ananias in a vision, and he answers, “Here I am.” Arminian commentators see a willing disciple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God using another believer in Saul’s conversion.

verses.text: The Lord said to him, “Arise and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying,
verses.arminianNotes: Go to Straight Street and ask for Saul of Tarsus, for he is praying. Arminian readers see prayer as evidence of Saul’s new direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that the persecutor now prays because God has changed him.

verses.text: and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul has seen Ananias in a vision coming to restore his sight. Arminian expositors see God preparing both men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God arranging every detail of the encounter.

verses.text: But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Ananias protests that Saul has done much harm to the saints. Arminian readers see honest fear expressed to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how unlikely Saul’s conversion appeared from a human view.

verses.text: Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul has authority to arrest all who call on Jesus’ name. Arminian commentators note the danger Ananias faces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see that God’s choice overrides every human calculation.

verses.text: But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: “He is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations, kings, and the children of Israel.” Arminian readers usually take this as election to service and mission, an appointment that Saul then freely embraced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul as a clear example of sovereign election, chosen and called while still an enemy, as he later says of himself in Galatians 1:15–16.

verses.text: For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Arminian expositors see a calling that will demand costly faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see suffering appointed as part of God’s plan for his servant.

verses.text: Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ananias lays hands on him, calls him “Brother Saul,” and says the Lord sent him so he may see and be filled with the Spirit. Arminian readers see grace extended through reconciliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the persecutor welcomed as family through God’s work.

verses.text: Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
verses.arminianNotes: Something like scales falls from his eyes; he sees again and is baptized. Arminian commentators see his baptism as his public response to Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see sight restored as a picture of spiritual illumination, followed by the sign of union with Christ.

verses.text: He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes: He eats, regains strength, and stays with the disciples. Arminian readers see the new believer joined to the community he once attacked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the converted persecutor received into the church.
